posts.body:
## Your session is really a set of if-then rules

When you start an operating session, every job goes back to square one and the board sorts the cards into four columns — Unavailable, Available, Running, and Finished. What decides where a job lands isn't you shuffling cards all night. It's the rules you set on each job ahead of time.

### Telling a job when it's ready

Each job can carry an "Available When" rule — one or more conditions joined by either *all of these* or *any of these*. A condition watches the rest of the board and waits for something to become true:

- another job has finished this session
- another job is running right now
- another job is *not* running
- a track is free
- a track is held

Leave the rule blank and the job simply uses its Available switch to decide whether it starts the session ready or waiting.

### A job follows its rule only until it runs

Before a job has run, its "Available When" rule is live — the board keeps re-checking it and slides the card between Unavailable and Available as conditions change. But the first time you run that job, the rule switches off for the rest of the session. From then on the card holds its place, and only two things can move it: starting it again, or a finish action from another job.

That's deliberate. Take an out-and-back turn: the outbound leg becomes available, you run it, and when it finishes its finish action flips the return leg to Available. Because the outbound job's rule has gone quiet, the leg stays parked in Finished instead of springing back to Available the moment its conditions happen to line up again.

### Finish actions: one job cueing the next

A finish action is a short list attached to a job that fires when that job wraps up. Each entry sets another job — or the finishing job itself — to Available or Unavailable. It's how you cue the next crew: finish the local, and the yard job it feeds suddenly shows up as ready. The one guardrail is that a finish action never pulls a job that's currently running, so nothing gets snatched out from under an operator mid-move.

### Keeping the floor sane

The board also holds two limits: how many jobs may run at once, and a smaller cap on how many of those can be WiFi throttles. Set them to match your crew and your gear, and the board won't hand out more work than the room can actually run.

posts.body:
## One app, two railroads

If you model more than one railroad — or you're starting a second one from scratch — you no longer need a separate app or a workaround to keep them apart. Track Runner now holds as many layouts as you like, and each one keeps its own equipment, locations, and operating records completely separate.

### Each layout keeps to itself

When a layout is active, everything you see belongs to it and nothing else — its locomotives, rolling stock, and inventory, its locations, tracks, and turnouts, and its jobs, sessions, and engineers. Two layouts can share no cars at all, or overlap however you like; the app never mixes them up. The banner at the top and your printed reports always show the name of whichever layout is active, so you're never guessing which railroad you're looking at.

### Switching, adding, and renaming

It all lives on the Layout screen in Settings. It lists every layout you've got; tap one to make it active, and the switch is instant — it's really just a filter, so there's no waiting and nothing to confirm. From the same screen you can add a new layout or rename an existing one. Deleting is deliberately careful: a layout has to be empty first. If it still owns records, the app tells you what's left instead of quietly discarding anything, and it won't let you delete the layout you're currently using or your last remaining one.

### What stays shared

A few things sensibly stay common across every layout, so you're not re-entering them each time: your lookup lists, your reference manuals, and your to-dos. Those follow you from layout to layout.

### Moving equipment between layouts

Sometimes a locomotive or a string of cars needs to move to another layout, and there are two ways to do it. **Move Shown to Layout…**, in the Manage menu on the roster and inventory lists, moves everything the screen is currently showing in one step — filter down to what you want, then send the batch across. For one-off moves, open a record, tap Edit, and use the **Transfer** button. Either way, your backups always include every layout, so nothing gets left behind.

posts.body:
## The wait is over — it's on the App Store

Model Railroad Record Keeper is now available on the App Store for iPad and Mac. If you've been keeping your layout's details scattered across notebooks, spreadsheets, and your memory, this is the app that pulls all of it into one place.

### What it does

It keeps everything about your railroad together — operating jobs, your full locomotive roster, the locations and tracks on your layout, inventory, to-dos, and a library of reference manuals. When you need it on paper, print a clean report for any of it.

### Yours, on your device

No account, no cloud, no sign-up. Everything lives on your device and works fully offline — whether you're at the workbench or out at a club layout with no signal.

### Where to get it

Open the App Store on your iPad or Mac and search for **Model Railroad Record Keeper**, or tap Download on the App Store from the homepage. That's it — you're running.
